=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Overall assessment

**The package is materially seller-favourable.** Its central weakness is that the Seller discloses unresolved risks, while proposing broad disclosure, buyer-knowledge and “all Claims” limitations that could leave the Buyer bearing those risks without an effective remedy.

The Seller’s statements that terms are “standard”, “FINAL” or agreed at principal level are **not evidence of Buyer approval**. Review every provision on its merits and verify any alleged agreement against the Buyer’s own records.

This assessment is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying SPA or DD documents. Those documents, including their definitions and cross-references, must be checked before settling drafting.

## Material issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Liability limitations extend far beyond general warranties

**Issue:** Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 purportedly apply limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance to **all Claims of any nature**. The proposed default application of time limits creates the same problem.

This could restrict claims for unpaid purchase-price adjustments, breach of completion obligations, specific indemnities, tax liabilities, title defects or misleading conduct—not just ordinary warranty breaches.

**Push back:**
- Confine the general warranty regime expressly to general warranty claims.
- Give tax, fundamental warranties and each specific indemnity their own expressly overriding regime.
- Preserve enforcement of payment obligations, completion obligations and appropriate equitable relief.
- Carve out fraud, fraudulent concealment and deliberate misconduct; scrutinise non-reliance language for its effect on misrepresentation and statutory remedies. Do not assume statutory claims can necessarily be excluded.
- Check every definition of “Claim” and every cross-reference: exceptions must survive the whole agreement, not merely clause 12.

### 2. The general warranty package materially limits recovery

**Issue:** A AUD 4.8 million cap is 20% of price. The AUD 250,000 deductible basket is approximately 1.04% of price, with a AUD 25,000 de minimis. Together, these leave the Buyer absorbing smaller losses and the first AUD 250,000 of qualifying losses. Eighteen months may miss issues emerging through subsequent reporting or renewal cycles.

These figures are negotiation positions—not inherently appropriate because the Seller calls them market terms.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher cap, lower thresholds and a **tipping basket**, under which qualifying losses become recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.
- Aggregate related claims so one underlying issue cannot be fragmented below the de minimis.
- Seek a longer notification period, for example 24 months, with separate longer periods where justified.
- Ensure timely notified claims survive expiry; avoid onerous notice particulars or a short deadline to commence proceedings.

The acceptable final package depends on diligence, available insurance and the Seller’s ability to pay.

### 3. Title, capacity, tax and IP should not all share the general regime

**Issue:** “Administrative simplicity” is no justification for limiting recovery for failure to deliver the ownership being purchased. Likewise, tax exposures can emerge well after 18 months, and core IP ownership is central to a SaaS acquisition.

**Push back:**
- Fundamental warranties covering capacity, authority, ownership and unencumbered transfer: no basket or de minimis, a substantially higher cap—seek at least the purchase price—and a materially longer claim period.
- A standalone tax covenant covering pre-Completion tax, with appropriate exclusions and claims mechanics, and survival aligned with relevant assessment and recovery periods.
- Strong IP ownership and infringement protections, with enhanced recourse where diligence identifies material exposure.
- Keep the Ironquay-specific protection separate from general IP warranties.

### 4. General disclosure and constructive buyer knowledge could neutralise warranties

**Issue:** Disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, accounts, registers and public records shifts the burden of identifying risks to the Buyer. Clause 8.3 goes further by imputing advisers’ knowledge and anything *discoverable*.

A document’s presence does not mean its commercial consequences were fairly explained. These provisions could defeat claims even where nobody on the Buyer team actually understood the issue.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**.
- Reject blanket incorporation of referenced documents and public records. If any general disclosure remains, narrowly define its scope.
- Freeze, index and retain the disclosed data-room set.
- Delete constructive knowledge and adviser imputation. If a knowledge exclusion is unavoidable, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, without deemed enquiry.
- Make clear that disclosure and knowledge do not qualify specific indemnities, fundamental protections or payment obligations unless expressly agreed.

**Crucially:** known risks need express allocation. A disclosed problem may no longer support a warranty claim.

### 5. Bluefen consent is not resolved

**Issue:** Bluefen accounts for approximately AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue. No final consent or evidence of satisfaction of its associated conditions is supplied. A reasonable-endeavours covenant does not deliver the required outcome; written consent alone may be conditional or commercially adverse.

**Push back:**
- Make satisfactory consent **and satisfaction of relevant conditions** a Buyer-waivable condition precedent.
- Require review of the executed consent and underlying clauses 11.2–11.3.
- Do not accept material fees, repricing, reduced rights or other adverse conditions without Buyer approval.
- Include a long-stop date and Buyer termination rights if the condition fails.

### 6. Riverlark debt and security must be cleared at Completion

**Issue:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding. A release supplied after Completion exposes the Buyer to acquired debt, continuing security and possible change-of-control consequences. That conflicts with a debt-free/cash-free acquisition unless properly dealt with in the price and completion mechanics.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a current lender payout letter covering principal, interest, fees and all secured obligations.
- Arrange direct repayment through Completion funds flow, with binding discharge/release arrangements effective at Completion and prompt registration mechanics.
- Cover all relevant securities, guarantees and related releases.
- Reconcile the debt deduction and repayment so the Buyer does not fund it twice.

### 7. Completion bonuses are an omitted economic liability

**Issue:** AUD 420,000 of conditional bonuses is absent from the funds flow. Calling this “a matter for the Seller” does not stop the acquired company becoming liable. Applicable on-costs are also unresolved.

**Push back:**
- Confirm the obligor, conditions, payment timing and applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.
- Allocate the agreed transaction-related burden to the Seller through payment, a price deduction or a specific indemnity.
- Reflect the treatment expressly in the funds flow and completion accounts, without double counting.
- Address bonuses payable after Completion because continued-employment conditions remain outstanding.

### 8. Ironquay protection is too narrow

**Issue:** The payment condition potentially affects ownership of SOW3 Project Materials, not merely an AUD 180,000 invoice. DD-010 is not conclusive evidence that the amount remains unpaid, but there is also no receipt or confirmatory assignment.

**Push back:**
- Verify payment status, all SOW3 fees and the scope and importance of the affected materials.
- Prefer a Completion deliverable comprising evidence of cleared payment and effective confirmation of ownership/assignment.
- Broaden the specific indemnity beyond the invoice to resulting title defects, third-party claims and reasonable remediation costs.
- Ensure that indemnity is not defeated by disclosure, knowledge, the general basket or the general claim period.

Do not assume payment alone cures every possible chain-of-title defect.

### 9. The export incident requires investigation—not dismissal or overstatement

**Issue:** The record establishes an unintended external delivery of a link potentially containing approximately 1,240 records. It does **not** establish access, a confirmed notifiable breach or quantified loss. Equally, the Seller has no adequate basis to dismiss it as immaterial.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the investigation, access logs, link permissions, containment evidence and confirmed data scope.
- Assess applicable privacy, contractual and notification obligations, including whether the Australian notifiable data breach regime applies.
- Require updates, preservation of evidence and appropriate consultation on remediation and communications.
- Seek a specific indemnity for agreed categories of pre-Completion incident exposure, including investigation, remediation and third-party claims, subject to lawful recoverability.
- Consider a Completion condition or retention if investigation reveals material unresolved exposure.

### 10. Sandbar renewals require economic analysis

**Issue:** Three related AUD 110,000 renewals total AUD 330,000. “Ordinary course” is not established. Their timing, service periods, cancellation rights and accounting treatment determine whether they are normal operating costs or a liability requiring adjustment.

**Push back:**
- Review DD-008 and DD-011 together and aggregate the commitments.
- Determine whether they are accrued liabilities, prepayments, debt-like items or future operating expenditure under the agreed price mechanics.
- Require Buyer consent for material new or renewed commitments before Completion.
- Avoid both assuming the full amount is deductible and allowing artificial splitting to evade consent thresholds.

### 11. Distinguish notification, assignment and share-sale consent requirements

- **Office lease:** The disclosed obligation is notification, not landlord consent. Verify the clause and require timely compliant notice.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not itself require consent to a share sale. Check for separate change-of-control provisions and any proposed restructuring or actual assignment.

Seek the protection the contracts require; do not create unnecessary consent dependencies.

### 12. The share register is insufficient standalone title diligence

**Issue:** DD-012 records the Seller as holder of all issued shares, but does not independently establish valid issuance, beneficial ownership, absence of encumbrances or absence of competing equity rights.

**Push back:** Reconcile the register with corporate records and capital history; verify options, convertibles and other rights; investigate relevant security interests; and obtain effective transfer documents, releases and fundamental warranties.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Protect Completion:** satisfactory Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/releases, verified share title and effective Ironquay ownership.
2. **Protect the economics:** include bonuses and on-costs, correctly treat debt and supplier commitments, and prevent double counting.
3. **Preserve recourse:** narrow the “all Claims” provisions, reject blanket disclosure and constructive knowledge, and separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes.
4. **Resolve known exposures:** obtain targeted Ironquay and incident protection, supported where appropriate by retention, escrow or credit support.
5. **Refresh diligence:** the disclosure snapshot is 22 September 2026. Require updated information through signing and Completion, without allowing unilateral supplemental disclosure to erase agreed remedies.

**Bottom line:** do not trade away enforceable remedies merely because risks have been disclosed. Resolve critical risks before Completion and expressly allocate the residual exposure to the Seller.
